I interview for finance roles and I will tell you the honest truth about what I am listening for, because it is not what most candidates prepare. I am not testing your accounting. Your CV already told me you can do the work, and the reference will tell me the rest. What I am working out in those forty minutes is whether you can explain something complicated to somebody who is not in your field, because that is eighty per cent of a senior finance job and it is the part nobody can teach quickly. So when you describe your current role, describe the shape of it. Who comes to you, and with what. What decision is yours and what decision is somebody else's. What happens in your process when you are on holiday. Those three answers tell me more than any qualification on the page, and almost nobody gives them.

The question that catches people is not the difficult one. It is: tell me about a strength. And almost everybody answers with an adjective. I am organised. I am detail-oriented. I am a fast learner. Those three sentences say nothing, and worse, they sound identical to the four candidates before you. What works is an adjective plus evidence, in one breath. I am the person who finds the difference before the auditor does, and last year that saved us three weeks of review. Now I have heard a strength and I have heard the proof of it, and I have not had to take your word for anything. Same with the weakness question, incidentally. Do not perform humility. Name something real, say what you are doing about it, and move on before it becomes the subject of the interview.
